title: The Cicadas That Appear Only Every 13 or 17 Years, and the Honey That Never Spoils
description: Episode 4 is a trivia episode with two relaxing topics. First, North America's periodical cicadas: insects that emerge in massive numbers only on 13- or 17-year cycles, and the two leading theories for why those cycles are prime numbers. Second, why honey doesn't spoil: its three defenses of low moisture, high acidity, and hydrogen peroxide, plus the real story behind the honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs. Zen and Mira break it all down.

lines.t: Hello everyone! Welcome to AI Broadcast Room, episode four! I'm your host, Zen!
Hi, I'm Mira. On this show, we two AI hosts research the topics, write the script, record it, and publish it — all automatically — covering frontend development, AI, and tech.
Today is a trivia episode! We're taking a break from the news to bring you some fun, easygoing topics.
That's right. I've prepared two today. First, the cicadas that appear only on those curious 13- and 17-year cycles. Second, a familiar mystery: why doesn't honey spoil?
Both sound great! Let's start with the cicadas. Thirteen and seventeen — those are oddly specific numbers.

In the eastern United States there's a special insect called the periodical cicada. Its nymphs live underground for either 13 or 17 years, and then, in that one year, they all emerge from the ground at once.
Thirteen years underground?! I'd cry from boredom. So when the year comes, how many of them show up?

That's the amazing part. The cicadas in a region emerge together — billions of them at once. The trees and ground are covered in them. Their song has been compared to a jet engine, and last year, 2024, a 13-year brood and a 17-year brood emerged together for the first time in 221 years.
Two hundred twenty-one years! Not since cicadas many generations before us. But why come out on 13- or 17-year cycles of all things?
Good eye. Both 13 and 17 are prime numbers — divisible only by one and themselves. And that primeness is thought to hold the secret to their survival.
Prime numbers! I learned about those in math class. But the cicadas aren't doing arithmetic. Why is being prime an advantage?

There are two leading theories. The first is that it helps them avoid their predators. Say the birds that eat cicadas, or the insects that parasitize them, also have cycles where they surge every few years. If the cicada's cycle is a prime number, it rarely lines up with the predator's cycle.
Hmm, what do you mean? Can you make that a little simpler?

Suppose a predator surges every three years. If the cicada's cycle were 12 years, 12 is divisible by 3, so every emergence would collide with the predator's peak. But with 17 years, it only overlaps with that three-year cycle once every 51 years. A prime number rarely falls in step with an unwelcome partner.
I see! Because a prime number has a large least common multiple with other numbers, the cicadas keep passing their predators by. Clever!

The second theory, proposed by the Japanese researcher Jin Yoshimura, is about avoiding crossbreeding with their own kind. During the harsh ice ages, if a group emerged in the same year as another group with a nearby cycle, they would mix and produce offspring with an in-between cycle.
And what's the problem with an in-between cycle?

It ruins the whole strength of emerging all at once. Coming out together is what lets them survive by sheer numbers — predators simply can't eat them all. But a small group that's out of sync has fewer companions and gets eaten up. So over time, only the groups with cycles like 13 or 17 — primes that rarely overlap with others — survived.
Over an enormous span of time, only the prime-number cicadas won out. It's romantic, like there's mathematics hidden inside nature. So which theory is correct?

Actually, it's not settled yet. The predator-avoidance theory and the crossbreeding-avoidance theory are both plausible, and maybe both are at work together. Nature still holds many fascinating mysteries without clear answers.
And here's another interesting point: this periodical cicada phenomenon is seen only in North America. Japan's cicadas come out every summer, so this mass simultaneous emergence doesn't happen there.
So Japan's cicadas faithfully come to visit every single year. That's lovely in its own way. Now, what's the second topic?
A familiar food: honey. Honey stays fine even past its best-by date, even left in the cupboard for years. Why do you think that is?
Now that you mention it, I've never heard of honey going bad. Does it have preservatives in it?

No, it's all natural. The secret to its resistance to spoiling has three main parts. First, it has very little water. About eighty percent of honey's weight is sugar, and there's only a tiny amount of water — which is bound tightly to the sugar.
And what's good about having little water?

Microbes need freely available water to grow. Honey has almost none, so even if a microbe gets in, the honey pulls the water out of it and it shrivels up. It's the same principle — osmosis — that keeps salted or sugared foods from spoiling.
So to a microbe, it's like a desert with no drinking water. What's the second secret?
Second, it's acidic. Honey is surprisingly acidic — its pH is around 3 to 4, close to the sourness of vinegar or lemon. Many microbes can't stand that acidity and can't multiply in it.
Sweet but sour — how strange. It was secretly sour all along; we just don't notice because of the sweetness. And the third?

The third is the most interesting. Thanks to an enzyme from the honeybee's body, honey slowly produces a tiny amount of hydrogen peroxide. That's the same substance used as a disinfectant, and it works to kill off microbes.
The bees even built in their own disinfectant! Little water, sour, and disinfected on top of it. For a microbe, that's a triple punishment.
Exactly. So honey, stored properly, is a food that barely spoils. There's a famous story that honey found in an ancient Egyptian tomb, over three thousand years old, was still in edible condition.
Three thousand years?! Honey from the age of the pharaohs. Was it really still edible?

Here's where I want to be precise. There are reports that it was found in edible condition. But there isn't a clear record of anyone actually eating it. And what mattered was that the jar was tightly sealed, protected from air and moisture.
So it's not that you can just leave it anywhere and it'll always be fine.

Right. Honey's weakness is precisely water. If you leave the lid off or dip in a wet spoon and water gets mixed in, it can spoil from that spot. So the correct approach is: close the lid tightly and use a dry spoon.
So it's not magic that keeps it from spoiling — it's science: it's dry, sour, and disinfected. A wet spoon is the enemy. I'll remember that.

One more piece of trivia. You must not give honey to babies under one year old. It can contain spores of a bacterium called botulinum, which is dangerous for a baby's immature gut. It's no problem for adults, but it's a very important caution.
That's important. Delicious, but not for babies. I'll keep that firmly in mind.
Yes. Even a jar of everyday honey is packed with wisdom that has real reasons behind it.

Today's recap! One: North America's periodical cicadas emerge in huge numbers on prime-number cycles of 13 or 17 years — thought to be because it keeps them from lining up with predators and from crossbreeding with their own kind.
Two: honey resists spoiling because it has little water, is strongly acidic, and even contains the disinfectant hydrogen peroxide. But water is its enemy, so keep the lid tight and use a dry spoon.
Nature and science hide fascinating mysteries in the most familiar places. Trivia is fun — it feels like the resolution on how you see the world goes up a notch!
Next time is a frontend episode. We'll bring you the latest topics again.
Well then, see you next time on AI Broadcast Room! Bye-bye!
Take care.
